title: The Lake That Killed 1,746 People in One Night
titles: The Lake That Killed 1,746 People in One Night
A Lake Exploded and Nobody Heard It
1,746 People Died in Their Sleep. The Killer Was a Lake.
description: On 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos in Cameroon released a silent cloud of carbon dioxide that killed 1,746 people and 3,500 cattle in one night. Rumors blamed a bomb, poison and angry spirits. Scientists found something stranger: a lake that can explode. This is the full story of the night, the warning that was ignored two years earlier at Lake Monoun, how the mystery was solved, and how scientists are defusing the killer lakes.

summary_short.say: In 1986, in Cameroon, more than seventeen hundred people went to sleep and never woke up. No fire. No flood. No sound. The next morning, a nearby lake had turned blood red. People blamed a secret bomb, poison, even spirits. The truth was stranger. The bottom of Lake Nyos was full of carbon dioxide, like a shaken soda bottle. That night, it burst. A heavy invisible cloud rolled down into the valleys and pushed out all the air. And two years earlier, a scientist had warned about this. His paper was rejected. Full story on the channel.

facts_to_check: Date: evening of 21 August 1986, around 9 pm; Lake Nyos, Northwest Region, Cameroon
Deaths: 1,746 people (often rounded to about 1,700-1,800), about 3,500 livestock, 845 injured (hospitalized figure)
CO2 released: estimates 100,000-300,000 tons (some older estimates higher); cloud about 1.2 cubic km, about 50 m thick
Cloud speed 20-50 km/h down the valleys; lethal up to about 25 km
Water/foam column about 100 m; wave at least 25 m; lake level dropped about 1 m; water turned red from iron
Lake Nyos depth about 208 m, roughly 1.8 km across
Villages: Nyos, Kam, Cha, Subum; survivors went to Wum; patients treated as far as Yaounde
Joseph Nkwain (Subum) quote: 'I could not speak. I became unconscious.'
Ephriam Che and Halima Suley (31 relatives) from Smithsonian Magazine 'Defusing Africa's Killer Lakes'
Lake Monoun: 15 August 1984, 37 dead; Haraldur Sigurdsson's paper rejected by Science in 1986 (Smithsonian)
George Kling sampled Nyos the year before; quote 'I was numb' (Smithsonian); Kling et al. Science 1987
Michel Halbwachs designed the degassing pipes; first permanent pipe January 2001; fountain about 45 m (148 ft); two more pipes in 2011
Natural dam (spillway) of Lake Nyos is weak; flood risk toward Nigeria reported by UN/experts
Lake Kivu about 2,000 times larger; about 2 million people near it; 2020 study found no increasing risk; methane power plant (KivuWatt)
Annual memorial on 21 August by survivors (verify)

scenes.say: On the night of August the twenty first, nineteen eighty six, in the hills of Cameroon, more than seventeen hundred people went to sleep... and never woke up.
There was no fire. No flood. No gunshots. The houses were standing. The food was still on the tables. Even the flies were dead.

lines: No fire. No flood. No gunshots.

scenes.say: And the killer was sitting quietly in the middle of the hills, looking exactly like it always had. A beautiful blue lake.
Good evening. This is one of the strangest mass deaths of the twentieth century. For weeks, nobody knew what had happened. People blamed a volcano, poison gas, even a secret bomb test.
The truth turned out to be stranger than all of them. And the most frightening part? It was natural. And it can happen again.
Lake Nyos sits high in the hills of northwest Cameroon, in West Africa. It fills the crater of an old volcano. It is small, less than two kilometers across... but more than two hundred meters deep.

Below the lake, the land falls away into green valleys. And in those valleys were villages. Nyos. Kam. Cha. Subum. Farmers grew maize and beans. Cattle herders, many of them Fulani families, grazed their animals on the slopes.

It was a peaceful place. But the local people had old stories about these crater lakes. Stories of lakes with spirits in them. Lakes that could rise up and kill. Some families had lived with those warnings for generations.
Scientists would later call these stories a kind of geomythology. Memories of real disasters, hidden inside legends. But in nineteen eighty six, almost nobody outside those hills took them seriously.

Thursday, August the twenty first. It was the rainy season, and the evening was cool. Around nine at night, people living near the lake heard a sound. Some said it was like a rumble. Others said like a gunshot, or a series of loud bangs.
A few people looked toward the lake and saw something rise from the water. A white cloud. Some described a mist. Some, a column of water and foam, shooting high into the air.

Scientists later estimated that column of water and foam reached about one hundred meters high. It sent a wave crashing against one shore, at least twenty five meters tall. It stripped the trees and grass off the hillside.
Then the cloud began to move. Not up into the sky, like smoke. Down. Down the hills, into the valleys, flowing along the ground like an invisible river.
It moved at twenty, maybe fifty kilometers an hour. About fifty meters thick. You could not outrun it in the dark. Most people never even knew it was coming.
It reached Nyos village first, and then Kam, Cha and Subum. It killed people up to about twenty five kilometers away from the lake.
Many died in their sleep. Some fell where they stood, in the middle of eating, or talking, or walking outside. It was quick. And it was completely silent.
When the sun rose the next morning, the valleys were quiet in a way no one had ever heard. No birds. No insects. No cattle calling.

A farmer named Joseph Nkwain, from Subum, had fallen unconscious. He woke up hours later, confused, unable to speak properly. His family members were dead around him. He managed to get on his motorcycle and ride to the town of Wum for help.

visuals.text: I could not speak. I became unconscious.

scenes.say: Others woke to the same horror. A farmer named Ephriam Che saw the mist rise from the lake. Later he found his family dead. In the years after, he raised his orphaned cousins himself.
A cattle herder named Halima Suley lost thirty one relatives, including her own children, in a single night. She survived. Her world did not.

The final count was one thousand seven hundred and forty six people dead. Around three thousand five hundred cattle. Hundreds more people were injured, with burns or blisters on their skin, breathing problems, and some could not move their arms or legs for a while.
About four thousand people fled the area. The injured were carried to hospitals, some as far as the capital, Yaounde.

visuals.quote: the 1986 news coverage of Lake Nyos

scenes.say: And the lake? The lake had changed color. The clear blue water was now a deep, rusty red. Its level had dropped by about a meter. As if something had come up from the bottom... and left.
Reporters arrived. One wrote that the place looked like the aftermath of a neutron bomb. Buildings standing, everything living gone.

visuals.text: Like the aftermath of a neutron bomb.

scenes.say: And the rumors started. Some said a foreign government had secretly tested a bomb or chemical weapon in the lake. Others said the government had poisoned the people. Others said the spirits of the lake had finally risen.

Some survivors remembered a smell. Like gunpowder, or rotten eggs. That pointed to volcanic gases like hydrogen sulfide. So the first big scientific suspect was obvious. The volcano under the lake had erupted.
Teams of scientists flew in from France, Britain, the United States, Japan and more. And they started to find problems with the volcano theory.
There was no fresh lava. No hot ash. The water was not hot. And when they tested the air and the water for sulfur gases, they found almost nothing.

lines: No lava. No ash. No heat.

scenes.say: What they found instead was in the deep water. When they pulled samples up from the bottom of the lake, the bottles fizzed. Some of them burst. Like shaking a bottle of soda and opening it.
The bottom of Lake Nyos was full of dissolved carbon dioxide. The same gas you breathe out. The same gas in a fizzy drink.
And here is the part that makes this story darker. This had already happened before. Two years earlier. And almost nobody listened.
On August the fifteenth, nineteen eighty four, at another crater lake called Lake Monoun, about a hundred kilometers away, thirty seven people were found dead along a road near the shore.
A volcanologist named Haraldur Sigurdsson, from the University of Rhode Island, went to investigate. He found no sign of an eruption. What he found was deep water loaded with carbon dioxide.

He wrote a paper describing what he called a hitherto unknown natural hazard. A lake that could release a deadly cloud of gas. In nineteen eighty six, he sent it to one of the most famous science journals in the world.
The journal rejected it.
Months later, Lake Nyos erupted. Nobody can say that one paper would have saved those villages. But the warning was there. Written down. Before the disaster.
So how does a lake kill seventeen hundred people? The answer is a disaster so rare that it needed a new name. A limnic eruption. A lake eruption.
Deep under Lake Nyos, there is still volcanic activity. Magma, far below, releases carbon dioxide. That gas seeps up through the rock and into springs at the bottom of the lake.

In most lakes, the water mixes. Warm and cold water swap places with the seasons, and any gas escapes slowly into the air. But Lake Nyos is deep, in the tropics, and protected by its crater walls. Its water barely mixes. The bottom layer stays at the bottom.

Down there, under the pressure of two hundred meters of water, carbon dioxide dissolves and stays dissolved. Year after year, the deep water absorbs more and more gas. Like a bottle of soda being filled... with the cap on tight.

Then something disturbs it. Nobody knows exactly what, on that night. Maybe a rockslide into the lake. Maybe cold rain cooling one side. Maybe strong wind. Some scientists think the lake was so unstable that it did not need any trigger at all.

Whatever it was, some deep water got pushed upward. As it rose, the pressure dropped. The gas came out as bubbles. The bubbles made the water lighter, so it rose faster, and released even more gas. A chain reaction. The whole lake opened like a shaken bottle.
Scientists estimate that between one hundred thousand and three hundred thousand tons of carbon dioxide escaped in a very short time. As a cloud, more than a cubic kilometer of gas.

visuals.label: of CO2, at the upper estimate

scenes.say: And here is why it killed. Carbon dioxide is about fifty percent heavier than air. So it did not drift away. It sank. It poured into the valleys and pushed the breathable air out of the way.

lines: It filled the valleys like water.

scenes.say: At low levels, carbon dioxide is harmless. You breathe it out right now. But at very high concentrations, a person loses consciousness within breaths. Without fresh air, they never wake up.

And the red water? Deep water at Nyos is rich in iron. When it rose to the surface and touched the air, the iron rusted. The whole lake turned the color of rust. The lake had turned itself inside out.
A young American scientist, George Kling, from the University of Michigan, had actually sampled Lake Nyos the year before the disaster. He came back after it. Later he remembered, I was numb.

Kling, Bill Evans of the U.S. Geological Survey and other teams published their findings in nineteen eighty seven. The mystery was solved. Not a bomb. Not poison. Not a spirit. The lake had suffocated its own valley.

And the case of Lake Monoun was solved with it. Two killer lakes, two years apart, same cause. Only two limnic eruptions have ever been recorded in history. Both in Cameroon. Both in the nineteen eighties.
But solving the mystery raised a terrifying question. The gas was still coming. The lake was already filling up again.
If the lake is a bottle of soda with the cap on, the solution sounds simple. Open the cap. Slowly.

A French engineer named Michel Halbwachs had an idea. Put a long pipe from the bottom of the lake to the surface. Pump a little water up to start it. Then, as gas bubbles out in the pipe, the water inside becomes lighter, and it keeps rising on its own. A self-powered fountain. Forever.

Not everyone believed it would work. Some scientists feared that disturbing the lake might trigger the very disaster they were trying to prevent. They tested small pipes in the early nineteen nineties. Then money ran out.

In January two thousand one, the first permanent pipe was switched on at Lake Nyos. It reached about two hundred meters deep. And it sent a fountain of water and gas shooting about forty five meters into the air.

visuals.quote: the degassing fountain at Lake Nyos

scenes.say: But one pipe was too slow. The lake was still taking in gas every year. In twenty eleven, two more pipes were added. Today, scientists say a large part of the dangerous gas has been removed, and the pipes can keep running without outside power.
Lake Monoun got pipes too. Two killer lakes. Defused, slowly, by a few scientists and a lot of patience.

But Nyos has another weakness. The natural wall that holds the lake in is made of loose volcanic rock, and it has been wearing away. If it ever collapsed, experts warned, it could send a flood into the valleys below, possibly as far as Nigeria.
Work has been done to strengthen that wall. But it is a reminder. Nyos was never just a story about gas. It is a story about how little we watch the places that can hurt us.
And there is a much bigger lake that scientists watch very carefully. Lake Kivu, on the border of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Lake Kivu is about two thousand times bigger than Nyos. Its deep water holds huge amounts of dissolved carbon dioxide and methane. And around two million people live near its shores.

Some studies once warned the gas was building up. A newer study, published in twenty twenty, corrected that and found no growing risk over time. Today, Rwanda actually pumps methane from Lake Kivu to make electricity, which also slowly removes gas from the lake.
And the survivors? Many were moved to new settlements away from the lake. Their land, their cattle, their homes were left behind. For years, the area around the lake was closed.
Some families slowly returned to farm near the valleys again. Others never went back. And many said the same thing. When the scientists leave, we live in fear.

scenes.say: Halima Suley, who lost thirty one relatives that night, rebuilt her life. She and her husband had more children. Life went on, because it had to.
Every year, survivors gather to remember the people who died on August the twenty first. The lake is still there. Blue again. Quiet again.
So what does Lake Nyos teach us? First. The most dangerous things are not always loud. The deadliest cloud of the twentieth century was invisible and made no sound.
Second. Old stories are sometimes data. The people around these lakes had warned about killer lakes for generations. The legends were right. The science just had not caught up.
And third. A warning only works if someone listens. In nineteen eighty four, the lake gave a warning. A scientist wrote it down. And it was rejected.
I'm Vix, and this case is closed. If you want more dark mysteries that science finally solved... you know what to do. Stay curious. And stay away from quiet lakes.
